references.text: Abraham shows hospitality to travelers by setting food before them, just as the host in Jesus' parable wishes to set food before his friend who has come from a journey.
Proverbs urges: "Do not say to your neighbor, 'Go away and come back,'" when you have something to give. This reflects the same commitment to helping a friend in need described in Luke 11:6.

"Good news from a distant land is like cold water for a thirsty soul." A friend who comes from far away has needs, and the host feels obligated to meet those needs—parallel to the situation in the parable.
The context of the verse: Jesus begins the parable about the friend who comes at midnight and knocks on the door asking for bread.
The continuation of the parable where the friend inside finally gets up and gives what is needed—not because of friendship, but because of the persistent request.
Jesus teaches about hospitality and setting food before guests, focusing on generosity—a theme that also underlies the parable in 11:6.
The exhortation not to forget hospitality, for by it some have unknowingly entertained angels. This reflects the deep commitment to hospitality that drives the host's desperation in Luke 11:6.
Paul urges believers to practice hospitality, which mirrors the same motive found in the parable—the obligation to care for traveling friends.
Peter exhorts believers to be hospitable to one another without grumbling, connecting to the hospitality assumed by the parable in Luke 11.
